sections.title: What Kubernetes Is and Why Container Orchestration Matters
sections.content: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scheduling, scaling, networking, and lifecycle management of containerized applications. Running containers directly with Docker can work for a small application, but production systems often contain many services, replicas, dependencies, and machines. Kubernetes provides a declarative control system where engineers describe the desired state of an application, such as the number of replicas, container image, resource requirements, and networking configuration. Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual cluster state match that declared state. If a container crashes, a controller can create a replacement. If a worker node becomes unavailable, workloads may be rescheduled onto healthy nodes when capacity and scheduling constraints allow. Kubernetes does not replace application development or container image creation. Instead, it provides a consistent platform for operating containerized workloads across infrastructure environments.

sections.title: Understanding Clusters, Nodes, Pods, and Workloads
sections.content: A Kubernetes cluster is a collection of control-plane services and worker nodes that cooperate to run applications. A node is a machine, virtual machine, or cloud-provided compute instance that contributes resources to the cluster. A Pod is the smallest deployable Kubernetes object and represents one or more closely related containers that share networking and may share storage. Containers inside the same Pod communicate through localhost and are scheduled together. Most application containers are managed through higher-level workload controllers rather than created as standalone Pods. A Deployment manages stateless application replicas and supports controlled updates. StatefulSets provide stable identities and storage relationships for stateful workloads. DaemonSets run a Pod on selected nodes, commonly for monitoring or networking agents. Jobs and CronJobs handle finite and scheduled tasks. Understanding these resource relationships helps engineers select the correct Kubernetes object instead of using Pods directly for every application requirement.

sections.title: Declarative Configuration and Desired-State Reconciliation
sections.content: Kubernetes uses declarative configuration to describe the state an application or infrastructure resource should maintain. A manifest commonly specifies an API version, resource kind, metadata, and specification. For example, a Deployment manifest can request three replicas of a particular container image and define resource requests, limits, labels, and health probes. When the manifest is submitted to the API Server, Kubernetes stores the desired configuration and controllers continuously compare that desired state with the observed cluster state. If one replica disappears, the Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers work to restore the requested replica count. This behavior is called reconciliation. It is different from a one-time command that starts a container and then stops managing it. Declarative workflows make changes reviewable, repeatable, and suitable for Git-based delivery. Teams should keep manifests in source control, validate them before deployment, and avoid uncontrolled manual changes that create drift between Git and the running cluster.

sections.title: Kubernetes API Objects, Manifests, and Resource Relationships
sections.content: Kubernetes manages cluster resources through API objects. Each object has an API group and version where applicable, a kind, metadata, and a specification describing its desired configuration. Common objects include Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Namespaces, PersistentVolumeClaims, and NetworkPolicies. Metadata supports identification and organization through names, labels, and annotations. Labels are especially important because selectors use them to associate related resources. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet manages Pods matching its selector. A Service selects matching Pods and provides a stable network endpoint even when individual Pod IP addresses change. ConfigMaps and Secrets provide configuration data to workloads through supported consumption methods. Engineers should understand these relationships before modifying manifests, because an incorrect label selector can leave a Service without endpoints or cause a controller to manage the wrong Pods. Use kubectl explain and API documentation to inspect resource fields and supported versions.

sections.title: Container Images, Registries, and Kubernetes Image Delivery
sections.content: Kubernetes runs containers from images stored in container registries. A Pod specification identifies the image repository and tag or digest, while the node's container runtime retrieves the required image when it is not already available locally. Production environments commonly use private registries such as Amazon ECR, Docker Hub private repositories, or enterprise registries. The cluster must have a supported authentication mechanism and network access to retrieve the image. An incorrect image name, missing tag, inaccessible registry, or insufficient permission can produce an ImagePullBackOff condition. Mutable tags can make deployments difficult to reproduce because the same tag may refer to different content over time. Digest-based image references identify a specific image artifact and improve release traceability. Teams should build and scan images in CI/CD, publish approved artifacts, and deploy known versions. Image pull permissions should be granted to the correct node or workload retrieval identity according to the Kubernetes platform and cloud integration being used.

sections.title: Scaling Applications and Maintaining Workload Availability
sections.content: Kubernetes supports application scaling by changing the number of workload replicas or by using autoscaling mechanisms. A Deployment can increase its replica count to run more copies of a stateless application, provided the cluster has enough scheduling capacity. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can adjust replica counts using configured metrics such as CPU utilization or supported custom metrics. Cluster-level autoscaling mechanisms can add or remove worker capacity when scheduling demand changes, depending on the infrastructure provider and configuration. Replicas improve availability only when workloads can be placed across suitable failure domains and the application itself supports multiple instances. Pod disruption budgets can help protect availability during voluntary disruptions, while readiness probes determine whether a Pod should receive normal Service traffic. Scaling also depends on resource requests, limits, application startup time, storage behavior, and downstream service capacity. Production teams should test scaling behavior under realistic traffic and avoid assuming that increasing replicas automatically resolves every performance bottleneck.

sections.title: Kubernetes Networking and Service Discovery Fundamentals
sections.content: Kubernetes provides a networking model in which Pods receive IP addresses and can communicate according to the cluster network implementation and configured network policies. Pod IP addresses are generally not stable across replacement, so applications should not depend on a specific Pod address. A Service provides a stable virtual endpoint and selects backend Pods using labels. ClusterIP is commonly used for internal cluster communication, while NodePort and LoadBalancer expose services through additional networking mechanisms. DNS-based service discovery allows workloads to resolve service names instead of maintaining changing IP addresses. Ingress resources and Gateway API implementations can provide HTTP or application routing through compatible controllers and infrastructure. Network policies can restrict Pod communication when the cluster networking implementation supports them. Engineers should understand the difference between Pod networking, Service routing, external load balancing, and DNS resolution when diagnosing connectivity. A service with no ready endpoints may indicate a selector mismatch, failing readiness probe, or unavailable Pods rather than a network outage.

sections.title: Storage, Configuration, and Application Health Management
sections.content: Kubernetes separates application configuration, sensitive values, and persistent data from the container image. ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration, while Secrets are intended for sensitive values and require appropriate access controls and encryption practices. Applications can consume configuration through environment variables or mounted volumes, depending on the resource definition and update behavior. PersistentVolumeClaims request storage from the cluster, while PersistentVolumes represent storage resources made available through the configured storage system. Storage behavior depends on the provisioner, StorageClass, access mode, and underlying storage capabilities. Applications should also define startup, readiness, and liveness probes according to their actual behavior. A startup probe can allow a slow application to initialize before other health checks become active. Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive Service traffic, while liveness can trigger container restarts when the configured failure condition is met. Poorly designed probes can cause unnecessary restarts or send traffic to an application that is not ready.

sections.title: Operating Kubernetes with kubectl and Production Best Practices
sections.content: kubectl is the standard command-line client for communicating with the Kubernetes API Server. Engineers use it to inspect cluster resources, apply manifests, retrieve logs, execute commands in containers, and diagnose workload conditions. Common commands include kubectl get, describe, apply, logs, exec, rollout, and top when metrics support is available. Always confirm the active context and namespace before running commands that modify production resources. Use namespaces and RBAC to separate teams and workloads, and grant only the permissions needed for each operational role. Store manifests in source control and use automated validation before applying changes. Monitor node health, Pod restarts, resource consumption, deployment progress, and application-level service indicators. Avoid treating kubectl apply as a complete deployment strategy without release validation, rollback planning, and change tracking. Production readiness also requires tested backups for relevant stateful data, secure image sources, network controls, resource planning, and documented incident procedures. These practices make Kubernetes operations more predictable and safer at scale.

sections.title: Kubernetes Control Plane and Worker Node Architecture
sections.content: Kubernetes architecture separates cluster management responsibilities from the execution of application workloads. The control plane maintains the cluster's desired state, exposes the Kubernetes API, makes scheduling decisions, and coordinates resource reconciliation. Worker nodes provide the compute environment where Pods run. In a self-managed cluster, engineers may operate control-plane components and worker machines themselves. Managed Kubernetes services operate some or most control-plane infrastructure on behalf of the customer, while customers remain responsible for workload configuration and many cluster-level decisions. A typical architecture includes the API Server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet, container runtime, and networking components. These components cooperate through the Kubernetes API and node-level communication. Understanding the separation of responsibilities is essential when diagnosing failures. For example, a healthy API Server does not guarantee that worker nodes can retrieve images, and healthy worker nodes do not guarantee that the scheduler can place new Pods. Production architecture must account for control-plane availability, worker capacity, network connectivity, identity, storage, and failure domains.

sections.title: Kubernetes API Server and Request Processing Lifecycle
sections.content: The Kubernetes API Server is the central entry point for cluster management operations. kubectl, controllers, automation systems, and other clients send API requests to it using authenticated and authorized connections. The API Server validates requests, performs admission processing, and coordinates persistence of accepted resource state in etcd. Authentication establishes the identity of the caller, while authorization determines whether that identity can perform the requested action on a resource. Admission controllers can validate or modify requests according to configured policies before persistence. This request path is important for security and troubleshooting because a request can fail at authentication, authorization, admission, validation, or storage. For example, an RBAC denial differs from an invalid manifest field or a failed admission policy. Engineers should inspect the actual API response and audit evidence rather than assuming every kubectl error indicates a control-plane outage. The API Server also provides discovery and resource endpoints used by clients and controllers to understand the available Kubernetes API surface.

sections.title: etcd as the Kubernetes Cluster State Database
sections.content: etcd is a distributed key-value data store used by Kubernetes to persist cluster state. Important information about Kubernetes API objects, including desired workload configuration and metadata, is stored through the API Server's persistence layer. The control plane relies on etcd availability and consistency to manage cluster state correctly. In self-managed environments, etcd deployment, member health, quorum, backup, encryption, and recovery are critical operational responsibilities. A multi-member etcd cluster can tolerate certain member failures while maintaining quorum, but losing quorum can prevent normal write operations. Managed Kubernetes offerings typically operate the control-plane data store as part of the service, so customers do not directly administer the provider's etcd infrastructure. However, they remain responsible for backing up application data and any cluster configuration that must be recoverable through their own processes. Never treat etcd as a substitute for application database backups. Understand the difference between Kubernetes control-plane state recovery and restoring persistent data used by applications.

sections.title: Kubernetes Scheduler and Pod Placement Decisions
sections.content: The Kubernetes scheduler assigns newly created Pods to suitable worker nodes. It evaluates resource requests, node capacity, scheduling constraints, affinity and anti-affinity rules, taints and tolerations, topology requirements, and other scheduling conditions. A Pod that cannot be placed remains pending while the scheduler waits for a suitable node or a change in cluster conditions. Resource requests are particularly important because they represent the capacity Kubernetes uses when evaluating placement. A node may appear to have free memory at the operating-system level but still lack allocatable capacity for the requested workload. Taints can repel Pods unless they have matching tolerations, while node selectors and affinity rules can restrict eligible nodes. Topology spread constraints can help distribute replicas across zones or nodes. Engineers should inspect Pod events with kubectl describe pod when scheduling fails. Increasing the replica count or changing node size without understanding the scheduling event may not solve the actual constraint. Effective capacity planning combines realistic resource requests with workload placement requirements.

sections.title: Controller Manager and the Reconciliation Architecture
sections.content: Kubernetes controllers continuously observe cluster resources and work to move actual state toward desired state. The controller manager runs several control loops responsible for different resource types and cluster functions. For example, a Deployment controller coordinates ReplicaSets, while a ReplicaSet controller ensures that the expected number of matching Pods exists. Other controllers manage endpoints, namespaces, service accounts, and node-related behavior depending on the cluster configuration. Controllers generally react to observed API state rather than executing a fixed sequence of commands only once. If a Pod disappears, the relevant controller notices the replica count difference and creates a replacement through the API. Reconciliation can take time, and it does not guarantee that every requested state is achievable. Missing resources, insufficient capacity, invalid specifications, or external dependency failures can prevent convergence. Engineers should inspect the controlling resource and its events rather than manually recreating managed Pods. Understanding controller ownership prevents conflicting manual actions and makes declarative operations more reliable.

sections.title: Kubelet and Node-Level Pod Lifecycle Management
sections.content: The kubelet is the primary node agent responsible for ensuring that Pods assigned to its node are running according to their specifications. It communicates with the API Server, observes Pod assignments, and coordinates container lifecycle operations through the configured container runtime. The kubelet also manages volume mounting, probe execution, and reporting node and Pod status. If a node loses communication with the control plane, the API Server may eventually mark the node unhealthy while the kubelet and running containers may continue operating locally for some time. Node-level failures can affect image retrieval, container startup, storage mounting, and health reporting. Engineers should inspect node conditions, kubelet logs, runtime health, disk pressure, memory pressure, and network connectivity when Pods fail on a particular worker. In managed services, access to the underlying kubelet may be restricted, so use the supported node diagnostics and provider logging facilities. Understanding kubelet responsibilities helps distinguish application failures from problems in the node's container execution layer.

sections.title: Container Runtime and CRI Integration
sections.content: Kubernetes uses a container runtime on worker nodes to create and manage containers. The Container Runtime Interface provides the integration contract between kubelet and supported runtimes. Common runtime implementations include containerd and CRI-O. Docker Engine was historically used in many Kubernetes environments, but Kubernetes removed its built-in dockershim integration in version 1.24; this did not mean that Docker-built images stopped working. OCI-compatible images can be used by supported runtimes when the image format and platform requirements are satisfied. The runtime is responsible for operations such as pulling images, creating containers, starting processes, and reporting container status through the CRI integration. Runtime failures can cause Pods to remain in creation states or fail during container startup even when the API Server and scheduler are healthy. Engineers should inspect runtime service health, node logs, image availability, storage capacity, and CRI compatibility. Avoid assuming that kubectl and Docker CLI commands provide identical views of every container on a Kubernetes node.

sections.title: Kubernetes Networking Components and Service Routing
sections.content: Kubernetes networking connects Pods, Services, nodes, and external clients through a combination of cluster networking and service-routing components. A Container Network Interface plugin provides Pod networking according to the cluster's implementation. Service routing may be handled by kube-proxy or an alternative supported data plane. kube-proxy watches Service and EndpointSlice information and configures node networking rules to direct traffic to appropriate backends. Different implementations may use iptables, IPVS, or other mechanisms depending on the environment and configuration. CoreDNS commonly provides service discovery by resolving cluster DNS names. In managed cloud clusters, additional cloud networking components may assign Pod addresses, integrate load balancers, or enforce network policy. A connectivity failure can occur at several layers: DNS resolution, Pod routing, Service selection, node rules, security groups, network ACLs, or external load balancer configuration. Troubleshooting should test each layer separately and verify that Service selectors match ready Pods. Architecture diagrams should show the actual networking implementation rather than assuming every cluster uses identical components.

sections.title: Control Plane High Availability and Failure Domains
sections.content: Production Kubernetes architecture must consider control-plane availability and the impact of failures across infrastructure and network boundaries. A highly available control plane distributes critical management services across suitable failure domains, depending on the Kubernetes distribution or managed service design. In self-managed clusters, engineers must plan API Server availability, etcd quorum, load balancing, certificates, backups, and recovery procedures. In managed services, the cloud provider operates the managed control plane, but customers still need resilient worker capacity and application placement. Worker nodes should be distributed across appropriate zones where the infrastructure and workload design support it. Pod replicas should avoid unnecessary concentration on a single node or failure domain. Pod disruption budgets and topology spread constraints can help reduce the risk of voluntary disruptions or uneven placement. High availability is not achieved merely by running multiple replicas if all replicas depend on one node, one storage system, or one network path. Validate the architecture through failure exercises that test node loss, zone impairment, capacity shortages, and application dependency behavior.

sections.title: Tracing an End-to-End Kubernetes Control and Workload Flow
sections.content: An end-to-end Kubernetes workflow begins when a user or automation client submits a workload manifest to the API Server. The request is authenticated, authorized, validated, and persisted as desired state. Controllers observe the new object and create dependent resources such as ReplicaSets and Pods. The scheduler selects suitable worker nodes based on resource requests, placement constraints, and node conditions. The API Server records the assignment, and the kubelet on the selected node observes the Pod specification. The kubelet asks the container runtime to retrieve required images and create the containers, while networking and storage components provide the necessary runtime resources. Health probes report application readiness and liveness, and Services route traffic to eligible endpoints. Controllers continue reconciling the workload if replicas disappear or configuration changes. When a deployment fails, engineers can trace the request through API validation, controller activity, scheduling events, node execution, image retrieval, storage mounting, and network routing. This layered mental model supports faster diagnosis because it identifies which component owns each stage of workload creation and operation.

sections.title: Amazon EKS Architecture Overview
sections.content:
## Amazon EKS Architecture Overview

### Technical explanation
Amazon EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes service. AWS operates the Kubernetes control plane, while the customer selects and operates workload capacity and configures the AWS resources surrounding the cluster. EKS architecture must be understood across the AWS account, VPC, cluster endpoint, IAM identity, worker compute, networking, storage, and application layers.

This section focuses on Amazon EKS Architecture Overview. Explain the overall managed Kubernetes architecture. Distinguish the AWS-operated control plane from customer-operated worker capacity, and describe how the cluster API connects these layers. The component or workflow must be understood as part of the complete Kubernetes request and reconciliation lifecycle rather than as an isolated feature. Engineers should identify which system owns each operation, which API object or AWS resource represents it, and which observable signal proves that it is functioning correctly.

### Internal workflow and component interaction
A typical operational flow begins when a user, controller, or automation tool submits a request through the Kubernetes API. The request is authenticated, authorized, validated, and processed by the relevant Kubernetes component. State changes are persisted where required, and controllers or node-level agents act on the resulting desired state. In EKS, AWS-managed infrastructure and customer-managed resources participate at different layers. Understanding these boundaries prevents engineers from troubleshooting an AWS-managed component as though it were a customer-operated Pod or EC2 process.

### Practical implementation and verification
Use the following command as a starting point:
aws eks describe-cluster --name production-eks --region ap-south-1

Run commands with the correct AWS profile, region, cluster context, namespace, and permissions. Inspect the returned object rather than assuming that a successful command means the application is healthy. Correlate Kubernetes events, resource conditions, AWS resource state, and application logs. In a production environment, capture the output and timestamp before changing configuration so that the original failure evidence remains available.

### Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Common failures include incorrect permissions, incompatible versions, missing network routes, exhausted resources, invalid configuration, unhealthy dependencies, and delayed reconciliation. Identify the failing layer first. Check whether the API request reached the cluster, whether the relevant object was accepted, whether the responsible controller or AWS integration acted, and whether the resulting workload or infrastructure became ready. Avoid deleting resources or changing multiple settings before collecting evidence.

### CI/CD and production engineering
A reliable delivery pipeline should validate manifests, verify image references, use narrowly scoped deployment identities, apply changes through controlled automation, and wait for rollout or resource readiness. Production teams should maintain version compatibility records, monitor resource capacity, protect secrets, restrict network exposure, and define rollback procedures. Changes to cluster infrastructure should be separated from application releases when their risk and recovery requirements differ.

### Operational checklist
Confirm ownership boundaries, permissions, dependencies, configuration, resource health, and monitoring. Record the expected state and compare it with the observed state. Verify that the relevant component is available, that its dependent services can communicate, and that failure signals are visible in logs or events. Document the corrective action and validate the application-level outcome before closing an incident.

## Kubernetes Worker Node Architecture

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes worker nodes provide the compute environment where application containers execute. In Amazon EKS, worker capacity can be supplied through managed node groups, self-managed EC2 instances, or Fargate for supported workloads. Node health directly affects scheduling, application availability, resource utilization, and recovery.

This section explains Kubernetes Worker Node Architecture. Explain the worker node as the execution environment for application Pods. Cover the operating system, kubelet, container runtime, networking components, storage integration, and the relationship with the Kubernetes control plane. These concepts are important because Kubernetes depends on clearly defined responsibilities between control-plane services, node-level agents, AWS integrations, and application workloads. A production engineer must understand not only what the component does, but also which resources it manages, which dependencies it requires, and how its health can be verified.

### 2. Internal operation and lifecycle
The operational lifecycle begins with a declared Kubernetes resource or an infrastructure configuration change. Relevant Kubernetes components observe the change, validate the required configuration, and perform their responsibilities. The resulting state is reflected through API objects, resource conditions, events, metrics, and logs. ## API Authorization and RBAC Request Decisions

### 1. Technical foundation
The Kubernetes API server exposes the cluster API, while etcd provides persistent storage for Kubernetes cluster state. This section explains API Authorization and RBAC Request Decisions. Explain how Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, and ClusterRoleBinding determine whether an authenticated identity can perform an API action on a resource. These concepts are important because Kubernetes depends on clearly defined responsibilities between control-plane services, node-level agents, AWS integrations, and application workloads. A production engineer must understand not only what the component does, but also which resources it manages, which dependencies it requires, and how its health can be verified.

### 2. Internal operation and lifecycle
The operational lifecycle begins with a declared Kubernetes resource or an infrastructure configuration change. Relevant Kubernetes components observe the change, validate the required configuration, and perform their responsibilities. The resulting state is reflected through API objects, resource conditions, events, metrics, and logs. In an EKS environment, AWS-managed infrastructure and customer-managed resources interact across the cluster boundary. Correct diagnosis requires identifying which layer owns the failing operation.

### 3. Practical implementation and commands
Start investigation with this command:

kubectl auth can-i get pods --all-namespaces

Use the correct cluster context, AWS region, namespace, and identity. Inspect the complete command output and compare it with the expected state. A command that exits successfully does not necessarily prove application health. For example, a Node object may exist while its kubelet is unhealthy, and an API endpoint may respond while a particular admission webhook or dependent service is failing.

### 4. Production troubleshooting
Investigate failures layer by layer. Check connectivity, identity permissions, component readiness, resource conditions, recent events, and dependency health. For worker-related problems, inspect node conditions, resource pressure, runtime status, and Pod placement. For API and state-related problems, inspect API readiness, request failures, authorization decisions, audit information, and available EKS control-plane logs. Preserve diagnostic evidence before applying disruptive changes.

### 5. Security and reliability practices
Apply least-privilege access, protect credentials, use supported software versions, and monitor resource and dependency health. Avoid granting broad permissions merely to bypass a failed request. Use controlled maintenance procedures, tested recovery plans, and documented ownership boundaries. In managed EKS environments, distinguish customer-configurable settings from infrastructure that AWS operates.

sections.title: Kubernetes Scheduling Architecture
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Scheduling Architecture

### 1. Technical foundation
The Kubernetes scheduler selects a suitable node for an unscheduled Pod, while the kubelet on that node coordinates the actual Pod execution. These are separate responsibilities: a successful scheduling decision assigns the Pod to a node, but it does not guarantee that images can be pulled, containers can start, volumes can mount, or health checks will pass.

This section explains Kubernetes Scheduling Architecture. Explain the scheduler's role in selecting a suitable worker node for every unscheduled Pod. Cover scheduler watches, scheduling cycles, binding, and the separation between making a placement decision and starting the container. Understanding this behavior helps engineers distinguish configuration errors from scheduling decisions, node execution problems, and application-level failures. Kubernetes continuously processes desired state, but different components own different stages of that process. A reliable investigation identifies the responsible component before changing resources or restarting workloads.

### 2. Internal workflow and component interaction
A typical lifecycle begins when a client submits a resource through the Kubernetes API. The API server validates and stores the object. Controllers may create or update dependent resources, and the scheduler makes placement decisions where scheduling is required. After assignment, the kubelet coordinates local execution through the container runtime and reports observed state. Networking, storage, security policies, and health checks contribute to the final workload outcome. A successful earlier stage does not prove that every later stage succeeded.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending

Use the correct kubeconfig context and namespace. Inspect the full output, events, conditions, and related objects. For a scheduling or node execution issue, compare the Pod specification with node capacity and node conditions. For a Pod lifecycle issue, inspect container state, restart count, image reference, probe configuration, mounted volumes, and recent logs. Verify the observed behavior instead of relying only on a successful apply operation.

### 4. Production troubleshooting
Common failure causes include insufficient resources, restrictive placement rules, unavailable images, invalid configuration, runtime errors, failed health probes, missing permissions, network restrictions, and storage attachment problems. Collect evidence using describe output, events, container logs, node status, and relevant AWS integration status. Change one cause at a time and verify the resulting state. Avoid deleting resources before understanding whether doing so could remove useful evidence or interrupt dependent workloads.

### 5. Security and reliability engineering
Use dedicated service accounts, least-privilege RBAC, controlled image sources, resource requests and limits, appropriate security contexts, and protected configuration. Design workloads to tolerate Pod replacement and node maintenance. Use readiness checks to control traffic eligibility, graceful termination to protect in-flight requests, and persistent storage for data that must survive Pod recreation. Do not treat a running container as proof that the application is ready or secure.

### 6. CI/CD and operational validation
A production pipeline should validate manifests, scan images, apply configuration through an approved identity, and wait for the required rollout or workload conditions. Capture deployment events and logs when validation fails. Confirm that the intended number of replicas becomes available, that application endpoints respond correctly, and that resource utilization remains within operational expectations. Keep rollback procedures and previous known-good configurations available.

### 7. Practical engineering checklist
Confirm the cluster context, namespace, resource specification, responsible controller, scheduling result, node health, runtime state, network connectivity, storage, security configuration, and application readiness. Compare expected and observed conditions, collect diagnostic evidence, apply the smallest safe fix, and verify the final user-facing behavior. Record the cause and preventive action so the same incident can be diagnosed faster in the future.

sections.content:
## Container States, Restarts, and Termination

### 1. Technical foundation
A Kubernetes Pod represents one or more tightly coupled containers that share selected execution resources and are scheduled as a unit. Pods are generally disposable: controllers create replacements when required, and a replacement Pod may receive a different name, UID, node, and IP address. Applications should therefore use stable Services and persistent storage where appropriate rather than depending on an individual Pod identity.

This section explains Container States, Restarts, and Termination. Explain Waiting, Running, and Terminated container states, exit codes, restart counts, restart policies, and how container lifecycle differs from the Pod lifecycle. Understanding this behavior helps engineers distinguish configuration errors from scheduling decisions, node execution problems, and application-level failures. Kubernetes continuously processes desired state, but different components own different stages of that process. A reliable investigation identifies the responsible component before changing resources or restarting workloads.

### 2. Internal workflow and component interaction
A typical lifecycle begins when a client submits a resource through the Kubernetes API. The API server validates and stores the object. Controllers may create or update dependent resources, and the scheduler makes placement decisions where scheduling is required. After assignment, the kubelet coordinates local execution through the container runtime and reports observed state. Networking, storage, security policies, and health checks contribute to the final workload outcome. A successful earlier stage does not prove that every later stage succeeded.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n production -o json

Use the correct kubeconfig context and namespace. Inspect the full output, events, conditions, and related objects. For a scheduling or node execution issue, compare the Pod specification with node capacity and node conditions. For a Pod lifecycle issue, inspect container state, restart count, image reference, probe configuration, mounted volumes, and recent logs. Verify the observed behavior instead of relying only on a successful apply operation.

### 4. Production troubleshooting
Common failure causes include insufficient resources, restrictive placement rules, unavailable images, invalid configuration, runtime errors, failed health probes, missing permissions, network restrictions, and storage attachment problems. Collect evidence using describe output, events, container logs, node status, and relevant AWS integration status. Change one cause at a time and verify the resulting state. Avoid deleting resources before understanding whether doing so could remove useful evidence or interrupt dependent workloads.

### 5. Security and reliability engineering
Use dedicated service accounts, least-privilege RBAC, controlled image sources, resource requests and limits, appropriate security contexts, and protected configuration. Design workloads to tolerate Pod replacement and node maintenance. Use readiness checks to control traffic eligibility, graceful termination to protect in-flight requests, and persistent storage for data that must survive Pod recreation. Do not treat a running container as proof that the application is ready or secure.

sections.title: Kubernetes Deployment Architecture
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Deployment Architecture

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes Deployments provide declarative management for stateless application workloads. A Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet maintains the required number of matching Pods. During updates, Kubernetes can create a new ReplicaSet and gradually move application capacity from an older revision to a newer one. This makes Deployment behavior central to safe CI/CD releases.

This section explains Kubernetes Deployment Architecture. Explain Deployment as a declarative workload controller that manages ReplicaSets and application rollout history. Describe how it maintains the desired number of replicas and supports controlled application updates. These mechanisms are important because application availability depends on more than creating Kubernetes objects. Engineers must understand the relationship between declared configuration, controllers, actual Pods, backend health, network routing, and application behavior. A resource can exist in the API while the intended workload or traffic path remains unhealthy.

### 2. Internal workflow and component interaction
A client submits the desired configuration through the Kubernetes API. The API server validates and stores the resource. Relevant controllers observe the change and reconcile dependent objects. For application releases, Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers coordinate Pod creation and replacement. For networking, Service selectors and endpoint controllers identify eligible backends, while the cluster networking dataplane forwards traffic. DNS provides names that clients can use without depending on temporary Pod addresses.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get deployments -n production

Use the intended kubeconfig context and namespace. Inspect the full resource specification, status conditions, events, and related objects. For a release, compare desired replicas with available replicas and inspect the active ReplicaSets. For traffic, compare Service selectors with Pod labels, inspect EndpointSlices, verify Service ports and target ports, and test name resolution and application connectivity from a suitable client Pod.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Common problems include mismatched labels, invalid selectors, insufficient cluster capacity, unavailable images, failed readiness probes, incomplete rollouts, missing endpoints, incorrect ports, DNS failures, and load balancer provisioning errors. Identify the layer where the expected behavior stops. Collect events and logs before modifying resources. Avoid repeatedly restarting workloads when the real issue is a missing endpoint, incorrect policy, or unavailable dependency.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Use least-privilege RBAC for release automation, trusted image registries, protected configuration, and appropriate Pod security settings. Expose only the required application ports. Prefer internal Services for internal communication and explicitly control external exposure. Use readiness checks, disruption budgets, capacity planning, monitoring, and documented rollback procedures to reduce the impact of releases and infrastructure changes.

### 6. CI/CD integration and release verification
A reliable pipeline should validate manifests, scan and publish images, apply approved changes, and wait for the intended rollout or traffic state. Capture the deployed image reference and revision. Verify that the required number of replicas is available and that clients can reach the correct application endpoint. For external traffic, also verify load balancer provisioning and backend target health rather than assuming that creating the Kubernetes Service completed the entire workflow.

### 7. Practical engineering checklist
Confirm the cluster context, namespace, resource selectors, desired state, controller ownership, replica availability, backend readiness, port mappings, DNS resolution, network permissions, and application response. Compare actual state with expected configuration, collect evidence, apply a targeted correction, and repeat validation. Document the cause and preventive improvement so that future releases and incidents can be handled consistently.

## Configuration Management in Kubernetes

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets allow workloads to consume configuration without embedding every environment-specific value into a container image. ConfigMaps are intended for non-confidential configuration. Secrets are designed for sensitive values such as credentials and certificates, but require appropriate encryption, access control, and operational handling. Both resources are namespace-scoped and must be referenced by workloads in the appropriate namespace.

This section covers Configuration Management in Kubernetes. Explain why application configuration should be separated from container images. Describe environment-specific configuration, declarative resources, immutable application artifacts, and how Kubernetes configuration objects support repeatable deployments. Understanding the behavior is essential because configuration errors and incorrect health signals can cause production incidents even when the Kubernetes API accepts the manifest. Engineers must verify the resource specification, actual container behavior, permissions, runtime state, and application response rather than assuming that a successful apply operation guarantees correct operation.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The user or deployment pipeline submits configuration through the API server. Kubernetes validates and stores the resource. Controllers and kubelet processes then act on the declared workload configuration. For configuration resources, the Pod specification determines how values are exposed to the application. For health probes, kubelet executes the configured check and updates container and Pod status. Service routing and Deployment availability consume relevant readiness information.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get configmaps -n production

Use the correct cluster context and namespace. Inspect the complete resource specification and related Pod details. Confirm that referenced keys and paths exist, the container can read required files, and configuration values are not accidentally printed into logs. For probes, verify the path, port, command, timeout, delay, and thresholds against the application's actual startup and response behavior. Review events and logs to correlate failures with application behavior.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Typical failures include missing ConfigMaps or Secrets, incorrect key names, namespace mismatches, failed volume mounts, insufficient permissions, stale process environment values, invalid credentials, probe timeouts, incorrect health endpoints, and restart loops. Collect Pod events, container logs, resource YAML, and relevant application evidence before changing the configuration. Make one targeted correction at a time and validate the result.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Use least-privilege RBAC and restrict access to sensitive resources. Avoid committing credentials to source control, embedding secrets in images, or printing secret values in pipeline output. Use encryption at rest where required and a documented rotation process. For health checks, keep endpoints lightweight and reliable, avoid exposing internal diagnostic information publicly, and prevent transient dependency failures from causing unnecessary container restarts.

A deployment pipeline should validate resource manifests, apply approved configuration changes, and verify the resulting Pod state. For configuration updates, confirm that the workload consumes the intended version and that restart or reload behavior is understood. For health probes, verify that the application becomes ready within the expected rollout window and that failures produce meaningful diagnostic evidence rather than uncontrolled restart cycles.

sections.title: Kubernetes Resource Management Fundamentals
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Resource Management Fundamentals

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes resource requests and limits describe the resource requirements and runtime constraints of containers. Requests influence scheduling decisions and capacity planning. CPU limits can restrict CPU execution through runtime throttling, while memory limits can lead to container termination when enforced memory usage exceeds the configured boundary. Correct sizing helps balance application performance, workload density, and infrastructure cost.

This section explains Kubernetes Resource Management Fundamentals. Explain how CPU and memory requests and limits describe workload resource requirements and constraints. Distinguish scheduling guarantees from runtime enforcement and show why resource configuration affects reliability, density, and cost. These concepts directly affect cluster reliability and security. Engineers should understand both the intended configuration and how Kubernetes enforces it at runtime. A valid manifest does not prove that a workload has sufficient capacity or that an identity has the correct permissions. Verification must include actual resource status, scheduler decisions, effective access, and operational evidence.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The API server validates and stores resource specifications. For resource management, the scheduler evaluates Pod requests against node allocatable capacity, while the container runtime and Linux resource controls enforce configured limits. For access control, authentication establishes the request identity and the authorization layer evaluates applicable RBAC rules and bindings. Namespace scope determines where namespaced objects and permissions apply.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get pods -n production

Use the intended cluster context and namespace. Inspect resource specifications, status, events, and related objects. For capacity analysis, compare requests and limits with observed usage, node allocatable resources, and scheduling events. For authorization analysis, inspect Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, service accounts, and the identity making the request. Test both the required permission and a sensitive action that should remain denied.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Typical problems include Pending Pods, insufficient CPU or memory, CPU throttling, OOMKilled containers, missing metrics, incorrect namespace selection, Forbidden API responses, incorrect API groups, and incomplete EKS identity mappings. Collect events, YAML, resource metrics, authorization output, and relevant logs. Identify whether the failure originates in scheduling, runtime enforcement, authentication, or authorization before changing configuration.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Use realistic resource sizing, capacity headroom, and namespace quotas to reduce resource contention. Apply least-privilege permissions, avoid wildcard RBAC rules, and restrict access to sensitive resources. Review privileged access regularly and keep emergency access controlled and auditable. Remember that namespaces do not replace network isolation, admission policies, or workload security controls.

### 6. CI/CD integration and operational control
A deployment pipeline should validate resource specifications and access requirements before applying changes. Resource policies should be tested against representative workloads and cluster capacity. RBAC changes should be reviewed as security-sensitive code, validated using permission checks, and applied through an approved identity. Record the target cluster, namespace, workload revision, and verification evidence for every production change.

### 7. Production engineering checklist
Verify cluster context, namespace, resource configuration, actual usage, allocatable capacity, workload status, applicable quotas, identity source, role rules, bindings, and effective permissions. Confirm that the application remains healthy and that access is no broader than required. Document the cause of any incident and introduce preventive policy, monitoring, or automated validation.

## Memory Limits and OOM Termination

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes resource requests and limits describe the resource requirements and runtime constraints of containers. Requests influence scheduling decisions and capacity planning. CPU limits can restrict CPU execution through runtime throttling, while memory limits can lead to container termination when enforced memory usage exceeds the configured boundary. Correct sizing helps balance application performance, workload density, and infrastructure cost.

This section explains Memory Limits and OOM Termination. Explain memory limit enforcement, container termination after exceeding the limit, OOMKilled status, exit code 137 as a common symptom, and the distinction between a container memory limit and node-wide memory pressure. These concepts directly affect cluster reliability and security. Engineers should understand both the intended configuration and how Kubernetes enforces it at runtime. A valid manifest does not prove that a workload has sufficient capacity or that an identity has the correct permissions. Verification must include actual resource status, scheduler decisions, effective access, and operational evidence.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The API server validates and stores resource specifications. For resource management, the scheduler evaluates Pod requests against node allocatable capacity, while the container runtime and Linux resource controls enforce configured limits. For access control, authentication establishes the request identity and the authorization layer evaluates applicable RBAC rules and bindings. Namespace scope determines where namespaced objects and permissions apply.

Start with this command:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n production

Use the intended cluster context and namespace. Inspect resource specifications, status, events, and related objects. sections.title: Resource Planning for Multi-Container Pods
sections.content:
## Resource Planning for Multi-Container Pods

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes resource requests and limits describe the resource requirements and runtime constraints of containers. Requests influence scheduling decisions and capacity planning. CPU limits can restrict CPU execution through runtime throttling, while memory limits can lead to container termination when enforced memory usage exceeds the configured boundary. Correct sizing helps balance application performance, workload density, and infrastructure cost.

This section explains Resource Planning for Multi-Container Pods. Explain per-container requests and limits, sidecar overhead, aggregate Pod scheduling requirements, init container resource considerations, and how logging or proxy sidecars affect workload capacity planning. These concepts directly affect cluster reliability and security. Engineers should understand both the intended configuration and how Kubernetes enforces it at runtime. A valid manifest does not prove that a workload has sufficient capacity or that an identity has the correct permissions. Verification must include actual resource status, scheduler decisions, effective access, and operational evidence.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The API server validates and stores resource specifications. For resource management, the scheduler evaluates Pod requests against node allocatable capacity, while the container runtime and Linux resource controls enforce configured limits. For access control, authentication establishes the request identity and the authorization layer evaluates applicable RBAC rules and bindings. Namespace scope determines where namespaced objects and permissions apply.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n production -o yaml

Use the intended cluster context and namespace. Inspect resource specifications, status, events, and related objects. For capacity analysis, compare requests and limits with observed usage, node allocatable resources, and scheduling events. For authorization analysis, inspect Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, service accounts, and the identity making the request. Test both the required permission and a sensitive action that should remain denied.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Typical problems include Pending Pods, insufficient CPU or memory, CPU throttling, OOMKilled containers, missing metrics, incorrect namespace selection, Forbidden API responses, incorrect API groups, and incomplete EKS identity mappings. Collect events, YAML, resource metrics, authorization output, and relevant logs. Identify whether the failure originates in scheduling, runtime enforcement, authentication, or authorization before changing configuration.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Use realistic resource sizing, capacity headroom, and namespace quotas to reduce resource contention. Apply least-privilege permissions, avoid wildcard RBAC rules, and restrict access to sensitive resources. Review privileged access regularly and keep emergency access controlled and auditable. Remember that namespaces do not replace network isolation, admission policies, or workload security controls.

sections.content:
## RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding

### 1. Technical foundation
Kubernetes namespaces organize namespaced resources into logical scopes, while Role-Based Access Control determines which authenticated identities can perform actions against the API. A Role or ClusterRole defines permissions, and a binding associates those permissions with users, groups, or service accounts. Namespace organization and RBAC are foundational to multi-team cluster governance, but must be combined with other security controls.

This section explains RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding. Explain how RoleBinding connects users, groups, or service accounts to a Role or ClusterRole within a namespace, while ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide scope. Include the security implications of each binding. These concepts directly affect cluster reliability and security. Engineers should understand both the intended configuration and how Kubernetes enforces it at runtime. A valid manifest does not prove that a workload has sufficient capacity or that an identity has the correct permissions. Verification must include actual resource status, scheduler decisions, effective access, and operational evidence.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The API server validates and stores resource specifications. For resource management, the scheduler evaluates Pod requests against node allocatable capacity, while the container runtime and Linux resource controls enforce configured limits. For access control, authentication establishes the request identity and the authorization layer evaluates applicable RBAC rules and bindings. Namespace scope determines where namespaced objects and permissions apply.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings

Use the intended cluster context and namespace. Inspect resource specifications, status, events, and related objects. For capacity analysis, compare requests and limits with observed usage, node allocatable resources, and scheduling events. For authorization analysis, inspect Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, service accounts, and the identity making the request. Test both the required permission and a sensitive action that should remain denied.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Typical problems include Pending Pods, insufficient CPU or memory, CPU throttling, OOMKilled containers, missing metrics, incorrect namespace selection, Forbidden API responses, incorrect API groups, and incomplete EKS identity mappings. Collect events, YAML, resource metrics, authorization output, and relevant logs. Identify whether the failure originates in scheduling, runtime enforcement, authentication, or authorization before changing configuration.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Use realistic resource sizing, capacity headroom, and namespace quotas to reduce resource contention. Apply least-privilege permissions, avoid wildcard RBAC rules, and restrict access to sensitive resources. Review privileged access regularly and keep emergency access controlled and auditable. Remember that namespaces do not replace network isolation, admission policies, or workload security controls.

### 6. CI/CD integration and operational control
A deployment pipeline should validate resource specifications and access requirements before applying changes. Resource policies should be tested against representative workloads and cluster capacity. RBAC changes should be reviewed as security-sensitive code, validated using permission checks, and applied through an approved identity. Record the target cluster, namespace, workload revision, and verification evidence for every production change.

Verify cluster context, namespace, resource configuration, actual usage, allocatable capacity, workload status, applicable quotas, identity source, role rules, bindings, and effective permissions. ## RBAC Auditing and Production Access Governance

### 1. Technical foundation

A Role or ClusterRole defines permissions, and a binding associates those permissions with users, groups, or service accounts. Namespace organization and RBAC are foundational to multi-team cluster governance, but must be combined with other security controls.

This section explains RBAC Auditing and Production Access Governance. Describe reviewing role rules and bindings, monitoring privileged access, audit logging, emergency access, identity lifecycle, access recertification, and safe revocation of permissions after team or workload changes. These concepts directly affect cluster reliability and security. Engineers should understand both the intended configuration and how Kubernetes enforces it at runtime. A valid manifest does not prove that a workload has sufficient capacity or that an identity has the correct permissions. Verification must include actual resource status, scheduler decisions, effective access, and operational evidence.

### 2. Kubernetes workflow and component interaction
The API server validates and stores resource specifications. For resource management, the scheduler evaluates Pod requests against node allocatable capacity, while the container runtime and Linux resource controls enforce configured limits. For access control, authentication establishes the request identity and the authorization layer evaluates applicable RBAC rules and bindings. kubectl get roles,rolebindings,clusterroles,clusterrolebindings

sections.title: Kubernetes Ingress Architecture and Traffic Flow
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Ingress Architecture and Traffic Flow

### 1. Technical foundation
Ingress defines HTTP and HTTPS routing rules for Kubernetes Services. An Ingress controller watches these resources and implements the rules using a proxy or cloud load balancer. In Amazon EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller can provision and manage Application Load Balancers for supported Ingress configurations. DNS, certificates, listener rules, target health, and backend readiness all participate in a working external request path.

This section covers Kubernetes Ingress Architecture and Traffic Flow. Explain Ingress as an API resource describing HTTP and HTTPS routing from external clients to Services. Describe the role of an Ingress controller, why creating an Ingress object alone does not provide routing, and how traffic reaches application Pods. Reliable network design requires understanding the complete packet path rather than checking only whether a Kubernetes resource exists. A successful API operation does not prove that DNS resolves, routes are correct, security controls permit traffic, certificates are trusted, or backend targets are healthy.

### 2. Component workflow and traffic path
For external application traffic, a client resolves a DNS name and connects to a load balancer or ingress endpoint. The controller reconciles Kubernetes routing configuration with the underlying proxy or AWS infrastructure. Traffic is matched against listener and routing rules, forwarded to a Service or registered backend, and ultimately delivered to an application Pod. For Pod networking, the CNI configures the network interface and address when the Pod sandbox is created, while node and VPC networking provide reachability.

### 3. Practical implementation and verification
Start with this command:

kubectl get ingress -A

Use the intended cluster context and namespace. Inspect controller status, resource specifications, Pod addresses, endpoint records, and relevant events. For an external route, verify DNS, listener configuration, certificate selection, load balancer address, target registration, and backend readiness. For CNI connectivity, inspect aws-node status and logs, node network interfaces, subnet address capacity, Pod IP allocation, and security rules.

### 4. Troubleshooting and failure analysis
Common failures include missing Ingress controllers, invalid IngressClass selection, absent backend endpoints, DNS errors, TLS mismatch, unhealthy load balancer targets, security group restrictions, failed Pod sandbox creation, IP exhaustion, and incorrect network policy rules. Follow the traffic path one layer at a time. Correlate Kubernetes events with controller logs and AWS networking evidence before making changes.

### 5. Security and production reliability
Expose only intended endpoints, enforce HTTPS where required, use managed certificate lifecycle practices, and restrict load balancer and security group access. Apply network policies where supported and validate their enforcement behavior. Plan subnet capacity with headroom for nodes, Pods, and growth. Use multi-AZ infrastructure and monitor address allocation, target health, and network errors.

### 6. CI/CD integration and operational control
Version-control Ingress, Service, controller configuration, and network policies. Validate manifests before deployment and review changes to public exposure, listener rules, security groups, and subnet dependencies. After rollout, verify DNS resolution, TLS negotiation, HTTP response behavior, backend target health, and Pod-level connectivity. Preserve a known-good configuration for controlled rollback.

### 7. Production engineering checklist
Confirm controller health, IngressClass, DNS records, listener rules, certificates, Service ports, EndpointSlices, Pod readiness, CNI health, Pod IP capacity, routes, security groups, and network policies. Test both expected access and prohibited access. Record packet-path evidence and implement monitoring or automated checks for the root cause.

sections.title: Kubernetes Storage Architecture
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Storage Architecture

### Technical Concept and Purpose
Explain the separation between ephemeral container filesystems, Pod volumes, and persistent storage resources. This concept is an important part of Persistent Storage because Kubernetes must coordinate application requirements with cluster infrastructure. Understand what resource or controller owns this behavior, which API objects describe it, and which component performs the actual operation. The configuration stored in the Kubernetes API represents the desired state; the responsible controller or node component works continuously to reconcile the actual state with that desired state.

### Kubernetes Workflow
Start by identifying the relevant Kubernetes objects and their relationships. Follow the lifecycle from the application specification through API validation, controller reconciliation, scheduling or resource allocation, and the final runtime behavior. Check which fields are required, which values are optional, and which defaults can influence the result. A successful API request does not always mean the workload has reached its intended operational state, so inspect both object specifications and their status conditions.

### Configuration and Practical Implementation
Use the following command as an initial inspection step:

kubectl get pods,pv,pvc,storageclass -A

Review the returned object carefully instead of relying only on its name or phase. Compare the configured values with the intended application behavior. In a real environment, use a version-controlled manifest, review changes before applying them, and make the smallest safe configuration change. Keep environment-specific values explicit and avoid copying production credentials or sensitive configuration into command history, logs, or shared manifests.

### Verification and Evidence Collection
Validate the result using Kubernetes object status, events, controller logs, and workload-level behavior. Check timestamps and namespace boundaries so that evidence belongs to the correct workload. When a resource remains Pending, Unknown, or otherwise unhealthy, inspect its events and dependencies before changing configuration. A healthy API response alone is not sufficient proof: confirm that the application can perform the operation it needs and that the result remains correct after a Pod restart or rescheduling event.

### Production Operations and Reliability
In production, evaluate availability, failure recovery, security boundaries, capacity, and operational ownership. Consider what happens during node replacement, zone failure, rolling deployment, controller restart, or a temporary loss of an external dependency. Define monitoring and alerting around meaningful symptoms rather than only object existence. Document the expected behavior, recovery procedure, and data or service impact so that another engineer can safely operate the system during an incident.

### Common Failure Modes and Troubleshooting
Typical failures include incorrect specifications, missing dependencies, incompatible configuration, insufficient permissions, unavailable infrastructure, and controller reconciliation errors. Use describe output and recent events to identify the earliest meaningful failure rather than repeatedly applying the same manifest. Confirm that the relevant Kubernetes component is healthy and that required APIs, drivers, metrics, network paths, and IAM permissions are available where applicable. Change one variable at a time and verify whether the observed condition improves.

### Engineering Best Practices
Keep manifests reviewable, use namespace-scoped access where possible, and apply resource limits and policies that match the workload's operational needs. Test configuration changes in a non-production environment before rollout. Record the expected state and measurable success criteria. For Persistent Storage, engineers should understand not only how to create the resource but also how to inspect its lifecycle, recognize failure signals, protect application availability, and recover safely without introducing unrelated changes.

sections.title: Deployment Rollout Fundamentals
sections.content:
## Deployment Rollout Fundamentals

### Technical Concept and Purpose
Explain how Kubernetes Deployments manage application versions through ReplicaSets and gradually replace existing Pods while maintaining the desired replica count. This capability is important in Rolling Updates and Rollbacks because production Kubernetes operations require predictable state transitions, controlled change management, and measurable service health. Understand the Kubernetes API objects involved, the controllers responsible for reconciliation, and the infrastructure dependencies that influence the result. The desired configuration describes what the platform should achieve, while the control plane and relevant AWS services coordinate the actual operation.

### Internal Workflow and Component Responsibilities
Follow the complete workflow rather than looking at only the final resource status. Identify the initiating API change, the controller that observes it, the dependent resources created or modified, and the node-level or AWS-level operations required to complete the activity. Separate control plane responsibilities from worker responsibilities. In EKS, also identify which responsibilities are managed by AWS and which remain under the cluster operator's control.

### Configuration and Practical Inspection
Start with this command:

kubectl get deployment,replicaset,pods -n <namespace>

Inspect the returned configuration and compare it with the intended operational state. Verify resource names, namespaces, versions, labels, annotations, permissions, and relevant status conditions. For production changes, prefer reviewed configuration and documented change procedures. Avoid making multiple unrelated changes during an incident because they make cause-and-effect analysis more difficult.

### Validation and Operational Evidence
Collect evidence from Kubernetes objects, events, controller logs, node conditions, and AWS service descriptions where applicable. Confirm that the change reached its intended state and that the application remains healthy. Check both control plane visibility and actual workload behavior. A successful command or accepted API request does not prove that all dependent components are healthy. Verify readiness, availability, service connectivity, and the relevant application-level success criteria.

### Reliability and Production Considerations
Evaluate availability, capacity, security, maintenance windows, and recovery options before performing the operation in a production cluster. Consider the impact of node replacement, zone-level failure, workload disruption, API unavailability, or an AWS dependency failure. Establish clear ownership for cluster-level and application-level responsibilities. Use monitoring and alerting to detect meaningful degradation, and document expected behavior so operators can distinguish normal reconciliation from an incident.

### Troubleshooting and Failure Analysis
Common failures include incorrect configuration, insufficient permissions, incompatible versions, unavailable infrastructure, controller errors, and resource constraints. Begin with the earliest relevant warning or failure event. Inspect the responsible component and its dependencies before retrying the operation. In EKS, distinguish Kubernetes errors from AWS IAM, EC2, VPC, load balancer, or managed-service errors. Correct the identified cause and verify recovery with fresh evidence.

### Engineering Best Practices
Use version-controlled configuration, least-privilege access, explicit change review, and repeatable operational procedures. Test disruptive operations in a non-production environment before production rollout. Maintain rollback or recovery plans appropriate to the operation, and record the state before and after changes. A production engineer should be able to explain the lifecycle, identify the responsible component, validate the result, and recover safely without introducing unnecessary disruption.

sections.title: Kubernetes Troubleshooting Methodology
sections.content:
## Kubernetes Troubleshooting Methodology

### Objective and Engineering Context
Explain a systematic incident investigation process that begins with symptoms, establishes scope, gathers evidence, and traces failures through Kubernetes dependencies. This subject is important to the final Stage 10 learning path because production Kubernetes and Amazon EKS environments combine application behavior, cluster control plane operations, AWS infrastructure, security controls, and operational processes. Understand the specific engineering problem, the expected result, and the boundaries of responsibility between Kubernetes, AWS-managed components, and application teams.

### Architecture and Component Relationships
Identify the Kubernetes resources, controllers, node-level components, and AWS services involved. Trace how information and requests move between these components. Distinguish desired state from observed state, and identify which component is responsible for each transition. For EKS, verify whether the relevant control plane capability is AWS-managed or whether the customer must operate an add-on, worker component, IAM configuration, or supporting AWS resource.

### Implementation and Investigation Workflow
Begin with the following command:

kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Use the output to establish the current state before making a change. Inspect resource specifications, status conditions, events, logs, and dependencies. For a production implementation, use reviewed manifests and infrastructure configuration rather than relying on undocumented manual changes. Keep the operation limited to the intended workload or cluster component, and record the original state so that later comparisons and recovery decisions are evidence-based.

### Validation and Acceptance Criteria
Define measurable success conditions before performing the operation. Verify API-level resource state, workload readiness, node health, network connectivity, and application behavior as appropriate to the topic. Confirm that dependent services remain available and that the change has not introduced unexpected resource consumption or security exposure. Repeat the relevant checks after a restart, rescheduling event, or controlled workload change when persistence and resilience are part of the requirement.

### Production Reliability and Security
Consider availability zones, capacity headroom, identity permissions, network boundaries, encryption, data durability, and failure recovery. Use least privilege and avoid embedding credentials in manifests or command output. Plan changes around workload disruption constraints and define the impact of partial failure. Production procedures should include ownership, monitoring, escalation criteria, and a safe recovery path rather than relying on an operator to improvise during an incident.

### Failure Scenarios and Corrective Actions
Potential failures include invalid configuration, missing permissions, unavailable dependencies, incompatible versions, resource exhaustion, failed scheduling, and controller reconciliation problems. Identify the earliest failure signal and correlate it with the relevant event, log, or AWS service status. Avoid deleting resources or restarting components before understanding their role and impact. Apply a targeted correction, then verify that the original symptom has disappeared and that related service behavior is healthy.

### Documentation and Operational Handover
Record the objective, prerequisites, configuration changes, commands executed, evidence collected, validation results, and known limitations. Include rollback or recovery instructions and identify the responsible team for each dependency. A useful handover enables another engineer to reproduce the validation, understand the architecture, and respond to a future incident without depending on undocumented knowledge.

### Advanced Engineering Exercise
Use this topic to build a repeatable exercise in a non-production environment. Establish a baseline, perform the operation or introduce a controlled failure, capture the observed behavior, and compare the result with the expected state. Evaluate whether monitoring detects the issue, whether recovery is safe, and whether the procedure protects application availability. Convert the findings into improvements to configuration, automation, documentation, or operational controls.
